name: Beautiful Mirrors with queries
description: Creatnx has $$$n$$$ mirrors, numbered from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$. Every day, Creatnx asks exactly one mirror "Am I beautiful?". The $$$i$$$-th mirror will tell Creatnx that he is beautiful with probability $$$\frac{p_i}{100}$$$ for all $$$1 \le i \le n$$$. Some mirrors are called checkpoints . Initially, only the $$$1$$$st mirror is a checkpoint. It remains a checkpoint all the time. Creatnx asks the mirrors one by one, starting from the $$$1$$$-st mirror. Every day, if he asks $$$i$$$-th mirror, there are two possibilities: The $$$i$$$-th mirror tells Creatnx that he is beautiful. In this case, if $$$i = n$$$ Creatnx will stop and become happy, otherwise he will continue asking the $$$i+1$$$-th mirror next day; In the other case, Creatnx will feel upset. The next day, Creatnx will start asking from the checkpoint with a maximal number that is less or equal to $$$i$$$ . There are some changes occur over time: some mirrors become new checkpoints and some mirrors are no longer checkpoints . You are given $$$q$$$ queries, each query is represented by an integer $$$u$$$: If the $$$u$$$-th mirror isn't a checkpoint then we set it as a checkpoint. Otherwise, the $$$u$$$-th mirror is no longer a checkpoint. After each query, you need to calculate the expected number of days until Creatnx becomes happy. Each of this numbers should be found by modulo $$$998244353$$$. Formally, let $$$M = 998244353$$$. It can be shown that the answer can be expressed as an irreducible fraction $$$\frac{p}{q}$$$, where $$$p$$$ and $$$q$$$ are integers and $$$q \not \equiv 0 \pmod{M}$$$. Output the integer equal to $$$p \cdot q^{-1} \bmod M$$$. In other words, output such an integer $$$x$$$ that $$$0 \le x \lt M$$$ and $$$x \cdot q \equiv p \pmod{M}$$$.
input_specification: The first line contains two integers $$$n$$$, $$$q$$$ ($$$2 \leq n, q \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$)  — the number of mirrors and queries. The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers: $$$p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$$$ ($$$1 \leq p_i \leq 100$$$). Each of $$$q$$$ following lines contains a single integer $$$u$$$ ($$$2 \leq u \leq n$$$) — next query.
output_specification: Print $$$q$$$ numbers – the answers after each query by modulo $$$998244353$$$.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1264C — Beautiful Mirrors with queries [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
